chunks: Connections needed to wire an op-amp. The question: What connections are required to wire up an opamp?
An op-amp needs a few connections before it does anything useful: power, two inputs, an output, a feedback path, and a decoupling capacitor.
Without feedback it works as a comparator (its output just slams high or low depending on which input is bigger), not as a smooth amplifier.
Without a defined steady (DC) voltage at each input, it drifts to a rail, one of the supply limits. And without decoupling, supply noise gets in.
Think of a lamp. It needs a power cord, a switch you control, and a bulb. A lamp with a loose cord flickers. Unplugging one wire leaves it dark.
In the same way, each missing op-amp connection gives its own symptom, from a stuck output to oscillation.

The seven connections: +supply, minus supply, two decoupling capacitors (one per supply, right at the pins), inverting input via R in , feedback R f from output to the inverting input, and a DC path for the + input (here, ground).
Signal path and power path are separate jobs.
Supply pins: V+ and Vminus . Vminus is ground in a single-supply design. Floating input: an input connected to nothing, which will drift.
Feedback path: a resistor from output to the minus input. Decoupling capacitor: usually 100 nanofarads at the supply pins, supplying fast current.
Common-mode range: the input voltages the part can handle.
Take a single 5 volts supply. Connect V+ to 5 volts with a 100 nanofarads capacitor right next to it, and Vminus to ground. Bias the plus input at 2.
5 volts with two equal resistors. Run a feedback resistor from the output to the minus input.
Now every pin has a defined connection, and the output has room to swing both ways around 2. 5 volts. That is the whole idea.
"Beyond the two inputs and the output, an op-amp needs a positive and negative supply, so power pins, with a 100 nanofarads decoupling capacitor close to them.
For a linear amplifier it also needs a feedback path from the output to the inverting input.
Both inputs need a DC path to a defined voltage, because bias current flows into them and a floating input drifts to a rail.
Then I check the common-mode range and output swing, and in single-supply designs I bias the signal to mid-rail."
